reasoning: Both outputs are strong Dev-Team PRDs that skip discovery, declare the output mode, build a holdout-based measurement plan, and flag open questions loudly. B wins on two dimensions that matter for the stated task ('engineering needs it Monday'). First, buildability: B specifies an explicit event taxonomy with in/out decisions and collapse rules per event type, a half-open window interval with a timezone offset snapshotted at scheduling time, an idempotency key, retry/backoff with an abandon rule, batch failure isolation, a concrete rollout ramp with spam-rate gates at each step, bounce/complaint/soft-bounce handling, read-replica generation, a permission regression test as a release gate, signed expiring unsubscribe tokens, email-verification eligibility, org-level admin disable, and accessibility requirements. A has none of the taxonomy, no retry/failure semantics, no ramp detail, no accessibility beyond P1 dark mode, and no email-verification or org-level controls. Critically, A identifies the 'digest complaints poison all company email' risk but prescribes only a kill switch; B prescribes the actual mitigation (D6: dedicated sending subdomain and ESP stream isolated from transactional, IP-warmed) plus a transactional-deliverability guardrail metric. A also leaves the timezone/batch-architecture question (OQ-3), which it calls the highest-cost question in the doc, unanswered on the critical path with an instruction to 'answer this before Monday' -- B decides it (D5) and prices the reversal as low. Second, factual accuracy under spot-check, which is where the two genuinely separate. A's headline external claim -- 'Google, Yahoo, Microsoft and Apple now enforce bulk-sender rules with hard rejection rather than spam-foldering' (repeated in section 4 as 'Enforcement is rejection, not spam-foldering') -- overstates a real trend into a blanket cross-provider absolute. Google's own sender guidelines FAQ still says 'Messages might be rejected or delivered to recipients' spam folders' and its enforcement table lists 'Temporary or Permanent Failure codes, or spam foldering'; Microsoft did move to hard 5.7.515 rejection, but Apple's documented enforcement still includes spam routing. A compounds this by generalizing Gmail's 0.30% figure to 'the platform hard limit' and 'any provider'. B scopes the same facts correctly ('per Gmail bulk-sender policy') and states the mitigation-eligibility detail verbatim-accurately: at 0.3%+ a sender is ineligible for mitigation until the rate stays below 0.3% for 7 consecutive days -- which matches Google's FAQ exactly. B's other cited claims also check out: CASL's 10-business-day unsubscribe window (CRTC), the CAN-SPAM primary-purpose test and transactional/relationship exemption (FTC), and the RFC 8058 one-click requirement. B's sourcing is materially better too: FTC and CRTC primary regulator pages and Google's own Help page, versus A's mostly vendor-blog citations (Red Sift, PowerDMARC, Mailgun, EmailLabs, TermsFeed). A is not wrong on everything it uniquely contributes -- its RFC 8058 gotcha (List-Unsubscribe and List-Unsubscribe-Post MUST be covered by the DKIM signature and in the h= tag, so adding them post-signing silently breaks one-click) is verified correct and is a real implementation trap B omits, and its Gmail ~102KB clipping rationale for the item cap is also verified. Those are genuine wins for A, but they are two details against B's broader and better-verified coverage. On the expectations both score 4/4: both switch straight to the document (B's one line of framing pushback explicitly accepts the build call rather than re-litigating it), both declare Dev-Team from the audience cue, both give measurable criteria anchored to a holdout and both explicitly disqualify open rate as a goal metric, and both name open questions rather than inventing answers -- A ordered by what they block, B grouped by owner with a separate decisions log carrying a cost-to-reverse column. A's edge is statistical rigor (pre-registering a minimum detectable lift, a 6-send evaluation window, and the exposure-adjustment problem raised in its stress test); B's is operational completeness and verified precision. The second matters more for a Monday engineering handoff, and the accuracy gap breaks the tie decisively in B's favor.

Verified-correct RFC 8058 implementation gotcha that B misses: List-Unsubscribe and List-Unsubscribe-Post must be added before DKIM signing so the signature covers them (RFC 8058 requires them in the h= tag), and the endpoint must accept an unauthenticated POST with no confirmation page
Verified-correct rationale for the item cap: Gmail clips messages over ~102KB behind 'View entire message', so an uncapped digest silently truncates for the heaviest users

Strongest statistical discipline of the two: pre-register a minimum detectable lift before send one, a 6-send evaluation window justified by cadence, and the exposure-adjustment problem raised honestly in the stress test
